units.title: Unit 39 — Global problems
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 82–83 (PDF pages 86–87).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: Society and institutions · environment, poverty and global challenges
learningObjectives: Describe environmental threats using natural combinations for climate change, pollution, energy and ecological damage.
Discuss poverty using precise verb–noun collocations, including the differences between alleviating and eradicating it.
Use appropriate expressions for migration, asylum, debt, natural disasters and child exploitation.
Recognise metaphorical and formal expressions in reports, campaigns and discussions of global problems.

items.example: Scientists continue to study how climate change affects coastal communities.
items.note: Climate change describes long-term shifts in climate patterns, including warming and changing rainfall.

items.example: Rising sea levels threaten several low-lying islands.
items.note: Rising modifies levels, not seas; the phrase describes an increasing average level of ocean water.

items.example: The new policy aims to reduce greenhouse gases produced by industry.
items.note: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere; the noun phrase commonly occurs with emit or reduce.

items.example: Removing a native species can disturb the ecological balance of an island.
items.note: Disturb here means disrupt a delicate relationship between species and their environment.

items.example: The wetland supports an ecological balance that depends on clean water.
items.note: A conventional pairing for the balance of relationships within an ecosystem.

items.pt: estoques pesqueiros; populações de peixes disponíveis para pesca
items.example: Local fish stocks have declined after years of intensive fishing.
items.note: In environmental and fishing contexts, stocks refers to the populations available in a particular area.

items.pt: combater a poluição; enfrentar o problema da poluição
items.example: The council introduced new measures to tackle pollution near the port.
items.note: Tackle means take action to deal with a problem, rather than simply discuss it.

items.pt: gases de escapamento; fumaça dos escapamentos
items.example: Cyclists complained about exhaust fumes on the busy road.
items.note: Fumes refers to gases or vapours; exhaust fumes come from vehicles and engines.

items.example: Many countries are trying to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels.
items.note: Coal, oil and natural gas are examples of fossil fuels.

items.example: Power stations that burn fossil fuels release gases into the atmosphere.
items.note: Burn fossil fuels is the natural verb–object combination for consuming fuels through combustion.

items.pt: dano irreparável; prejuízo impossível de reparar
items.example: The chemical spill caused irreparable damage to the lake.
items.note: Irreparable means that damage cannot be repaired; irreversible damage is a close alternative.

items.pt: reduzir a camada de ozônio; causar a diminuição da camada de ozônio
items.example: Certain chemicals can deplete the ozone layer if released into the air.
items.note: Deplete means reduce a resource or layer substantially; do not confuse ozone depletion with the greenhouse effect.

items.example: International agreements have helped protect the ozone layer.
items.note: The ozone layer absorbs much of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet radiation.

items.pt: aderir à política ambientalista; adotar propostas políticas verdes
items.example: The party decided to embrace green politics in its new manifesto.
items.note: Embrace means support or adopt enthusiastically; green politics focuses on environmental concerns.

items.example: Green politics became a major issue during the election campaign.
items.note: A broad expression for political approaches centred on environmental protection.

items.example: Urgent measures are needed to protect the drinking-water supply.
items.note: Measures is a formal noun for actions or policies intended to address a problem.

items.example: The authorities introduced short-term measures while planning a permanent solution.
items.note: Short-term refers to immediate or temporary actions; contrast with long-term strategies.

items.pt: as safras fracassam; as plantações não produzem
items.example: When crops fail, farming families may lose most of their income.
items.note: A crop fails when it produces little or no usable harvest, often because of adverse conditions.

items.pt: fome devastadora; crise de fome catastrófica
items.example: Years of conflict and drought caused a devastating famine.
items.note: Devastating emphasises extremely harmful consequences; famine is a widespread severe shortage of food.

items.example: Devastating floods damaged roads and displaced thousands of residents.
items.note: The adjective highlights the destructive impact of widespread flooding.

items.example: Emergency teams train to respond to natural disasters such as earthquakes and floods.
items.note: A broad category for destructive events linked to natural processes; human activity can affect their impacts.

items.pt: sair da pobreza; escapar da pobreza
items.example: Access to reliable work can help families escape poverty.
items.note: Escape poverty means leave a condition of deprivation, not physically escape from a place.

items.pt: viver abaixo da linha da pobreza
items.example: Many households continue to live below the poverty line despite working full time.
items.note: The poverty line is an income or consumption threshold defined for a particular context.

items.example: The report compares household income with the national poverty line.
items.note: A conventional economic and social-policy term; the threshold varies by definition and country.

items.example: Better access to education can help lift people out of poverty.
items.note: Lift out of poverty is a common figurative phrase for improving people’s economic circumstances.

items.word: a widening gulf between rich and poor
items.pt: desigualdade crescente entre ricos e pobres
items.example: The study points to a widening gulf between rich and poor in the region.
items.note: A fixed metaphor for a growing social or economic divide between income groups.

items.example: New transport links could improve access to services in deprived regions.
items.note: Deprived describes places lacking resources and opportunities; it need not mean that every resident is poor.

items.pt: as margens da sociedade; situação de exclusão social
items.example: The programme aims to support people living on the margins of society.
items.note: Margins is figurative, referring to exclusion from opportunities or participation in mainstream society.

items.pt: dormir ao relento; dormir na rua
items.example: The charity provides blankets to people who sleep rough during winter.
items.note: A chiefly British expression for sleeping outdoors without adequate accommodation.

items.example: Local organisations provide education and support for street children.
items.note: An established but broad expression for children who live or spend substantial time on the streets.

items.example: After the storm, several villages were in desperate need of clean water.
items.note: Desperate intensifies need, indicating that help or resources are urgently required.

items.example: The editorial argues that social conditions breed crime when opportunities are scarce.
items.note: Breed metaphorically means give rise to; this wording states a debated causal claim, not an inevitable rule.

items.pt: a economia mundial; a economia global
items.example: A sharp rise in energy prices can affect the global economy.
items.note: Global economy refers to economic activity and connections across countries.

items.pt: uma oportunidade de ouro; uma excelente oportunidade
items.example: The new funding provides a golden opportunity to improve public transport.
items.note: Golden is figurative: an unusually promising chance, rather than anything made of gold.

items.example: Community organisations are working together to combat poverty.
items.note: Combat is a somewhat formal alternative to tackle or fight in policy discussions.

items.pt: erradicar a pobreza; eliminar completamente a pobreza
items.example: The organisation has a long-term goal to eradicate poverty.
items.note: Eradicate means remove completely, a stronger claim than alleviate poverty.

items.pt: reduzir a pobreza; amenizar a situação de pobreza
items.example: The cash-transfer programme is intended to alleviate poverty among older residents.
items.note: Alleviate means make a problem less serious; it does not necessarily mean eliminate it.

items.example: There is rarely a simple solution to a complex social problem.
items.note: Solution is normally followed by to when naming the problem being solved.

items.example: Many developing countries face difficulties financing major infrastructure projects.
items.note: A widely used economic classification; exact groupings depend on the organisation and indicator.

items.example: Some journalists seek political asylum after receiving serious threats.
items.note: Seek political asylum means request protection in another country because of persecution or danger.

items.pt: solicitantes de asilo; pessoas que pedem proteção internacional
items.example: Asylum seekers may have to wait for a decision on their applications.
items.note: An asylum seeker has requested protection; this status is not identical to having been recognised as a refugee.

items.example: Economic migrants may move abroad in search of better employment opportunities.
items.note: This expression emphasises economic motives; individual migration circumstances can be more complex.

items.pt: ir às ruas para protestar; sair às ruas
items.example: Residents took to the streets to demand safer roads.
items.note: A figurative set phrase commonly used for public protests or demonstrations.

items.example: Thousands gathered to demonstrate against the proposed cuts.
items.note: Demonstrate against identifies what protesters oppose; demonstrate for can indicate support.

items.pt: pagamentos da dívida; parcelas de amortização da dívida
items.example: Rising interest rates increased the country’s debt repayments.
items.note: Debt repayments refers to payments made to pay back money owed, often with interest.

items.pt: um número enorme de mortos; elevado saldo de mortes
items.example: The earthquake left a massive death toll and widespread destruction.
items.note: Death toll means the number of people killed by an event; massive emphasises a very high count.

items.example: If an earthquake hits a region with weak buildings, the damage can be severe.
items.note: Hit is a common journalistic verb for disasters affecting a place.

items.example: The campaign calls for stronger enforcement of laws against child labour.
items.note: Labour uses British spelling; the collocation concerns work performed by children, particularly harmful or exploitative work.

items.example: The charity works to prevent the sexual exploitation of children.
items.note: A formal expression used when discussing a serious violation of children’s rights.

items.example: The researchers collected samples to measure marine pollution near the harbour.
items.note: Marine is an adjective meaning relating to the sea; marine pollution concerns contamination of oceans or seas.

sectionsChecked: A · The environment: climate change, greenhouse gases, pollution, fossil fuels, failed crops and extreme events
B · Poverty: the poverty line, unequal opportunities, social exclusion, homelessness and economic measures
C · Other global problems: asylum, migration, public protest, disaster impacts and children’s rights

units.title: Unit 40 — Time
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 84–85 (PDF pages 88–89).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · time expressions, schedules, past and future
learningObjectives: Use common verb–noun collocations with time to discuss duration, planning, efficiency and leisure.
Distinguish spend, waste, save, make, kill and take in time-related expressions.
Describe life periods, early or late working hours, deadlines and future possibilities using natural fixed phrases.
Notice register differences and common learner errors, including run out of time versus run off time and have a good time versus spend a good time.

items.example: I like to spend time outdoors after a busy week.
items.note: Spend time is the natural expression for devoting time to an activity; pass time differs in meaning.

items.example: Do not waste time searching for files without checking the folder names.
items.note: Waste means use time unproductively; also collocates with money and resources.

items.example: Using a clear template can save time when preparing reports.
items.note: Save time means reduce how long a task takes, in contrast to waste time.

items.example: Could you tell me the time before the meeting starts?
items.note: The conventional pattern is tell someone the time, not tell the hour; me makes the target natural for TTS.

items.example: She uses her free time to practise English and read novels.
items.note: Free time is time when you are not occupied by work or other obligations.

items.example: He repairs old bicycles in his spare time.
items.note: Spare time and free time have similar meanings; in my spare time is especially common.

items.example: I hope to have time to finish the report today.
items.note: The grammar is have time to followed by an infinitive; use have time for before a noun.

items.pt: ter tempo para; dedicar tempo a
items.example: I always try to have time for my closest friends.
items.note: Follow for with a noun or noun phrase; contrast have time to do something.

items.pt: reservar tempo para; arranjar tempo para
items.example: Even during deadlines, she tries to make time for exercise.
items.note: Make time for means deliberately create room in a busy schedule; for is required.

items.pt: matar tempo; passar o tempo enquanto espera
items.example: We played cards to kill time before our train arrived.
items.note: Informal idiom for filling spare moments while waiting for something else.

items.pt: fazer com calma; não ter pressa
items.example: Take your time reviewing the contract before signing it.
items.note: An invitation to proceed without rushing; it does not mean take someone else’s time.

items.example: The technician arrived right on time for the appointment.
items.note: Right on time stresses punctuality; it is fairly neutral in tone.

items.example: The show started bang on time despite the rain.
items.note: Bang is a very informal British intensifier for exactly on time.

items.example: The coach left dead on time, so nobody had to wait.
items.note: Dead intensifies exact punctuality and is informal here; it does not refer to death.

items.example: We had a good time at the weekend festival.
items.note: Say have a good time, not spend a good time, when meaning enjoy yourself.

items.example: I hope you have a great time on your holiday.
items.note: Have a great time is an emphatic alternative to have a good time.

items.word: have the time of your life
items.pt: divertir-se como nunca; ter a melhor experiência da vida
items.example: He had the time of his life during his first trip abroad.
items.note: An idiomatic, enthusiastic phrase for an exceptionally enjoyable experience.

items.example: As time goes by, her confidence in speaking English increases.
items.note: A common expression for gradual change as time passes.

items.pt: à medida que o tempo passa
items.example: As time passes, old photographs often become more meaningful.
items.note: A natural alternative to as time goes by; it tends to sound slightly more neutral.

items.pt: ficar sem tempo; esgotar o tempo disponível
items.example: We ran out of time before discussing the final question.
items.note: Run out of time means no time remains; run off time is not idiomatic.

items.pt: pra valer; muito; de forma intensa
items.example: The company underestimated the costs and lost money big time.
items.note: An informal adverbial phrase meaning to a very great extent, often following a verb.

items.pt: passar o tempo; distrair-se enquanto espera
items.example: Reading short stories can help pass the time on a long flight.
items.note: Pass the time means occupy time, often while waiting; spend time need not imply waiting.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: The past few weeks have been particularly busy at work.
items.note: Past modifies a recent period leading up to now; the phrase normally takes plural weeks.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: Their grown-up children now live in different cities.
items.note: Grown-up is an adjective meaning adult; the hyphen is conventional before a noun.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: The exhibition explores digital art from the early 21st century.
items.note: Early refers to the beginning of a historical period; 21st is pronounced twenty-first.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: The museum displays tools that people used in prehistoric times.
items.note: Prehistoric times refers to periods before the development of written historical records.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: The documentary compares modern transport with developments in the recent past.
items.note: Recent past refers to a period not long ago rather than a distant historical era.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: The organiser warned everyone about possible last-minute changes.
items.note: Last-minute is hyphenated before a noun and describes something happening very close to a deadline.

items.pt: ajustar o despertador; programar o alarme
items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: Remember to set your alarm before going to bed.
items.note: Set means program the alarm to sound at a particular time; it does not mean switch it off.

items.pt: o alarme dispara; o despertador toca
items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: The alarm goes off at six every weekday.
items.note: For an alarm, go off means ring or sound; this is different from a device switching off.

items.pt: do amanhecer ao anoitecer; do nascer ao pôr do sol
items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: During harvest season, many workers are busy from dawn till dusk.
items.note: The fixed expression means all day; reversing the nouns changes the intended time span.

items.pt: a madrugada; as primeiras horas da madrugada
items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: They stayed awake talking until the small hours.
items.note: A British expression for the very early hours after midnight, especially around two to four.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: He was tired of answering work calls at ungodly hours.
items.note: An informal, disapproving expression for extremely early or late hours.

items.pt: demorar uma eternidade; levar muito tempo
items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: It takes ages to upload large files over this slow connection.
items.note: Informal: take ages means take a very long time, not literally several historical ages.

items.pt: valer a pena; compensar o tempo e o esforço
items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: The training course will be worth your while if you use the new skills.
items.note: Often used with be, make it or find it; the meaning is that the benefit justifies the effort.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: The young engineer seems to have a great future ahead of her.
items.note: Ahead is a metaphor for coming years; the pattern is have a great future ahead of you.

items.pt: um futuro não muito distante; futuro próximo
items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: We hope to release the new version in the not too distant future.
items.note: A conventional phrase for a relatively near future without specifying an exact date.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: Nobody knows exactly what the future holds for this technology.
items.note: Hold is metaphorical: the future may bring unknown events or developments.

items.section: B · Past, future and working hours
items.example: I stayed up late to finish the assignment.
items.note: Stay up means remain awake rather than go to bed; late describes the bedtime.

items.pt: dispor de um minuto; ter um minutinho livre
items.example: Could you spare a minute to check this figure?
items.note: A polite request for a small amount of someone’s available time.

items.word: at the end of the day
items.pt: no fim das contas; no final do dia
items.example: At the end of the day, we need a solution that users can understand.
items.note: Often a figurative discourse expression meaning ultimately; it can also refer literally to evening.

items.example: In this day and age, many people expect services to work online.
items.note: A conventional phrase meaning in modern times, sometimes used to express surprise or criticism.

items.pt: trabalhar em horários inconvenientes; trabalhar em horários que prejudicam a vida social
items.example: Emergency staff often work antisocial hours, including nights and weekends.
items.note: In British English, antisocial hours refers to working times outside standard daytime schedules.

items.example: She prefers to work regular hours so she can plan her evenings.
items.note: Regular hours contrasts with irregular shifts or unusually early or late work.

items.example: The old clock strikes every hour in the town square.
items.note: Strike is the conventional verb for a clock sounding the hour with chimes or bells.

items.pt: os minutos passam lentamente; os minutos vão passando
items.example: The minutes tick by as the team waits for the results.
items.note: Tick by evokes the movement or sound of a clock and the passage of time.

B · Past and future: recent and prehistoric times, working hours, alarms, deadlines and expectations
